A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their main text, Tables 1–3, and Appendices A–E can be matched. However, v2 page 24 contains only an external-availability notice for an absent figure, mnist.png. Its contents cannot be assessed from the supplied PDFs.

before.justification: Section 6 and Tables 1–3 report original experiments on graph anomaly detection, Wasserstein-distance prediction, and neural-network weight alignment.

after.justification: Section 6 retains these original experiments and reports revised numerical results in Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The irreducible-decomposition approach, equivariant layer constructions, and non-Siamese components remain unchanged. Both versions use the same restricted within-weight/bias-space couplings for alignment. The new suggestion to use automatic computational methods is not documented as an implemented component.

E1.justification: The dataset and task families remain unchanged, including all Wasserstein datasets and MNIST/CIFAR10 alignment. Table 1 makes a limited revision to graph test conditions by replacing noise variance η=0.2 with η=0.1 while retaining noise-free evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 1's 'Single non-Siamese' comparator is renamed 'DSS'; both passages identify the same additional mapping from Wang et al. and Maron et al. NProductNet remains the Wasserstein comparator, and the Siamese method from Navon et al. remains the alignment comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes the reported Wasserstein training budget from 40 to 200 epochs, a substantial fivefold revision. Table 1 also replaces η=0.2 with η=0.1. Alignment training remains 100 epochs. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The readable material retains the same layer-component comparisons and Wasserstein input-size generalization tests, while revising graph-noise robustness from η=0.2 to η=0.1. The unavailable mnist.png referenced on v2 page 24 prevents determining whether additional alignment analysis was added or how substantial it is.

E5.justification: The readable results retain point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The unchanged counts of 27 graph configurations and four alignment configurations describe hyperparameter searches, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All three result tables change. On clean graphs, Siamese accuracy changes from 50% to 10%, and the single-non-Siamese/DSS result from 99% to 97.5%. Table 2 revises eight SchurNet entries under the longer reported training budget; NProductNet values remain unchanged. Table 3 reverses the MNIST Acc(↓) ranking: SchurNet/Siamese change from 1.0e-5/4.0e-5 to 1.5e-5/1.25e-5, although SchurNet retains lower losses. Results under changed noise or training budgets are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Lemma E.1 corrects the irreducibility statement's group from G^k to G wreath S_k, with corresponding clarification around Theorem 5.1; the lemma's proof still initially states only G^k invariance. Section 3 adds the two- or four-dimensional non-absolutely-irreducible case. Section 5 replaces the explicit semidirect-product description with product notation. The principal decompositions and remaining proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: alternative layer derivations, simpler weight-space characterization, general wreath-equivariant layers, and empirical benefits. More consistent use of '2-IGN' clarifies a restriction already explicit in v1 Section 4.2.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies case-specific irreducible decomposition as the methodological bottleneck, discusses applicability to compact groups, and suggests computational assistance outside absolute irreducibility. The conclusion specifically identifies higher-order k-IGN decomposition as future work. The alignment motivation also softens the prior claim of recovering original-network performance to obtaining better interpolation results.

D1.justification: Appendix A revises the documented Wasserstein training duration from 40 to 200 epochs. The remaining implementation disclosures, including optimizers, graph-layer width, hyperparameter-search counts, learning-rate/weight-decay information, and the code link, are unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. However, Section 3 newly positions the already-cited Finzi et al. method as a computational complement for non-absolutely-irreducible representations. The central relationships to DeepSets, 2-IGN, weight-space networks, and prior transitive wreath-product characterizations remain intact.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose and terminology revisions and adds explanatory paragraphs. The small-n graph discussion moves from Section 4.2 to Appendix C.3 without substantive removal. The overall narrative structure remains stable, with updated publication-header text and an extraneous formatting-template page appended.

P2.justification: The author block, citation colors, table sizing, captions, and emphasis change. Table 2 moves from page 10 to the bottom of page 9, where its caption extends beyond the page boundary and its surrounding paragraph continues awkwardly on page 10. v2 also appends the missing-figure notice and formatting-template page; no additional scientific figure is actually visible.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies applicability and corrects Lemma E.1's statement, but its updated results are not consistently integrated. Table 1 reports identical 10% Siamese accuracies despite prose claiming lower accuracy with noise; Table 3 favors Siamese on MNIST Acc(↓) despite the retained claim of SchurNet winning in all settings. Table 2 also develops a layout defect. These competing benefits and harms, together with the unavailable MNIST figure, prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
